Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Residue proximity information and protein model discrimination using saturation-suppressor mutagenesis" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by John Kuriyan (Senior editor) and three reviewers. The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Your manuscript has been read and discussed by three reviewers and the editor, and the decision is the work is, in principle, acceptable for publication in eLife. There are, however, a number of issues with the manuscript, as written, that can be improved by judicious editing. These issues are outlined below, and we ask that they be addressed in a revised manuscript. The revised manuscript will be handled by the editor, without further external review.

1) One of the reviewers is still not convinced that the method you use to distinguish between proximal/distal pairs, and to identify active site residues, is robust. You have provided a manuscript that has been submitted elsewhere that addresses the underlying concepts. Please provide a more complete justification for these points in the present manuscript, so that a non-specialist reader can fully understand the logic behind the method. Cite the submitted manuscript as appropriate. Refer to standard methods of analysis where appropriate, rather than to methods developed in your lab.

2) This reviewer is also not convinced that the superiority of this method is clearly demonstrated by the limited set of decoy calculations done and by the one EV-fold comparison that is provided. On the whole, though, we feel that these comparisons are useful, but you could make it more clear in the manuscript that these are illustrative differences rather than definitive demonstrations of superiority. Please point out limitations of the comparisons.

3) The manuscript is quite difficult for a non-specialist to follow, and in this way it obscures the innovation and depth of the work. It is essential that the manuscript be edited so that it is accessible to a generally knowledgeable structural biologist or biochemist. Some of the points to note are listed below, but it is recommended that the revised manuscript be read by a seasoned non-specialist colleague, and their advice taken, before being resubmitted to eLife.

A) The manuscript is heavy on long run-on paragraphs that introduce multiple ideas, making it difficult for the reader to follow. Break up the flow into separate paragraphs for each idea, concept or result.

B) Ideas are introduced out of order, often with highly specific and cryptic information provided before a more general explanation. For example, CcdB is used without explanation first. Later, concerning CcdB, the incomprehensible statement (to a non-specialist) that "This is <5L" is made. Only later is the biological function explained, and the "<5L" statement is never explained. This is but one of several such instances that make the paper difficult for a general audience.

C) Please avoid the use of inessential abbreviations – we are not under page limits in an online publication. For example, it is highly recommended that "parent inactivating mutation" be spelt out everywhere – the editor sees no reason why this should not be done, and the use of PIM is felt to add to the incomprehensibility of the manuscript. Likewise, why use SSM when it can be spelt out? Why abbreviate yeast surface display with the incomprehensible YSD? The editor asks that you retain only standard abbreviations or gene names.

D) Please ensure that all metrics are clearly explained to the non-specialist reader. For example, in the subsection “Discrimination between proximal and distal suppressors “"RankScore" is used with no explanation.

results.result: A saturation-suppressor mutagenesis methodology was developed for CcdB, where five inactive mutants at buried residues (V5F, V18W, V20F, L36A, L83S) were selected as parent inactive mutants, and exhaustive second-site saturation mutagenesis libraries were constructed and screened using yeast surface display and FACS to identify suppressors. The library construction methodology effectively introduced parent inactive mutants into all members of the single-site saturation library, and after multiple rounds of sorting, 1-3 potential suppressors were identified for each parent inactive mutant, yielding six residue pairs containing parent inactive mutants and putative proximal suppressors.
results.evaluation: The claims describe a comprehensive experimental workflow that is well-documented with specific details about library construction (C74-C76, C101), screening methodology (C77-C78), and quantitative outcomes (C80-C81, C106). The methodology is validated by the successful identification of suppressors for four of five parent inactive mutants, and the library design is shown to effectively introduce parent inactive mutations throughout the library (C79). The experimental approach is internally consistent and the results are reproducible.

results.result: Proximal and distal suppressors can be accurately discriminated based on RankScore values from the single-site saturation mutagenesis library, where RankScore correlates with residue depth. Suppressors with RankScore=1 were classified as distal (R10, E11), while those with RankScore≥25 were classified as proximal. All six identified proximal suppressor pairs had shortest distances of 2.8-4.8 Å in the crystal structure, while distal suppressors R10 and E11 were 11.6-18.4 Å from their respective parent inactive mutants and located on an exposed loop.
results.evaluation: The discrimination method is well-validated by mapping suppressors onto the known crystal structure (C107, C110, C111). The RankScore parameter was previously established to correlate with residue depth (C90), and the cutoffs chosen (RankScore=1 for distal, ≥25 for proximal) are justified by structural data showing that all residues with RankScore≥25 have depth>5.5Å and accessibility<1.5% (C99-C100). The spatial validation confirms the accuracy of the classification method.

results.result: Experimentally identified proximal pairs were used to define a ContactScore metric that recovered >98% of native-like models (backbone RMSD within 2.5Å) from a decoy dataset of 10,659 CcdB models. ContactScore performed significantly better than the rdepthscore metric, recovering 100%, 98%, and 80% of structures in RMSD ranges 1.5-2Å, 2-2.5Å, and 2.5-3Å respectively, compared to 0%, 7%, and 12% for rdepthscore. ContactScore identified 585 models with RMSD<4Å (66% recovery) compared to only 67 models (8% recovery) for rdepthscore.
results.evaluation: The model discrimination analysis is well-designed with a large decoy set (10,659 models) spanning a wide RMSD range (1.9-20.4Å). The ContactScore metric is clearly defined (C146-C147) and shows excellent performance with quantitative comparisons to an alternative metric (C154-C156). The high recovery rates for low-RMSD models and the progressive decrease in recovery with increasing RMSD demonstrate the sensitivity and specificity of the approach. The results are internally consistent and the metric is properly validated.

results.result: Identified CcdB suppressors conferred improved binding affinity to DNA Gyrase and increased thermal stability to parent inactive mutants. All (parent inactive mutant, suppressor) pairs except (L36A, M63L) and (L36A, R10G) showed increased Gyrase affinity, while all pairs except (V20F, E11R) showed increased surface expression. The distal suppressor R10G increased surface expression when paired with V5F, V18W, L36A, and L83S, demonstrating that R10G acts as a global suppressor.
results.evaluation: The characterization of suppressors is comprehensive, with binding affinity measurements (C116), thermal stability data (C117), and surface expression analysis (C119-C120). The identification of R10G as a global suppressor is well-supported by testing it against multiple parent inactive mutants (C123-C124). The exceptions noted (C116, C120) are properly documented and explained. The correlation between surface expression and stability is supported by prior literature (C118), strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: The distal suppressor R10G shows unique properties: it increases CcdB stability relative to WT (Tm=74.8±0.2°C vs 66.8±1.0°C) but shows decreased affinity for the antitoxin CcdA (only 9°C Tm increase with CcdA vs >20°C for other mutants). R10 contacts CcdA in the crystal structure (2.9Å hydrogen bond to N69), explaining why mutations at this position destabilize CcdA binding. This represents an evolutionary trade-off between stability and function, explaining why R10G is not found in natural CcdB homologs.
results.evaluation: The characterization of R10G is thorough, combining thermal stability measurements (C133), ligand binding analysis (C126-C128), and structural interpretation (C130-C132). The evolutionary explanation (C135-C136) is well-reasoned and consistent with the data showing that R10G increases stability but compromises antitoxin binding. The screen design (C137) appropriately explains why this mutation was identified despite not being naturally occurring. The mechanistic understanding is coherent and well-supported.

results.result: For the membrane protein DgkA, which has two significantly different structures (X-ray PDB 3ZE5 and NMR PDB 2KDC), suppressor methodology was applied to residues with differential contacts in the two structures. At all five tested parent inactive mutants (V62Q, M66L, M66S, I67V, V68G), suppressors were found only at positions in contact with the parent inactive mutant in the X-ray structure, with no suppressors found at positions proximal only in the NMR structure. This indicates the X-ray structure represents the functional, in vivo conformation.
results.evaluation: The experimental design is elegant, using differential contacts between two structures to discriminate which represents the functional conformation (C164-C166). The results are unambiguous: all six identified suppressor pairs (V62Q/A41G, M66L/V38A, M66S/G35A, I67V/I103L, I67V/A104T, V68G/A100V) are consistent only with the X-ray structure (C168). The reproducibility is documented (C170: >5 independent experiments per mutant). The only exception (W112V, C169) is reasonably explained by the large volume change. The conclusion is strongly supported by the data.

results.result: Computational coevolution analysis of DgkA (4175 sequences) using DCA, GREMLIN, PSICOV, EVfold, and SCA showed that predictions were more consistent with the X-ray structure than the NMR structure. Of six experimentally identified contacts, three (62-41, 67-104, 68-100) were predicted by GREMLIN, PSICOV, and EVfold, only one (67-104) by DCA, and none by SCA. This demonstrates that sequence coevolution and suppressor mutagenesis provide complementary information.
results.evaluation: The computational analysis is comprehensive, using five different coevolution methods (C173-C174). The agreement between computational predictions and the X-ray structure (C176, C242) provides independent validation of the suppressor results. The partial overlap between experimental and computational contacts (C177-C179) is honestly reported and supports the conclusion that the approaches are complementary (C180). The large number of sequences (4175) makes DgkA suitable for computational analysis, unlike CcdB.

results.result: Active-site and buried residues can be distinguished based on mutational sensitivity patterns: buried positions show low MSseq for aliphatic substitutions and high MSseq for polar/charged substitutions, while active-site positions show high MSseq for most substitutions including aliphatic residues. Using this approach, nine residues (Q2, F3, Y6, S22, I24, N95, W99, G100, I101) were identified as putative active-site residues in CcdB based solely on mutational data, and similar patterns were observed in PDZ domain and GB1.
results.evaluation: The discrimination method is based on clear, interpretable patterns in mutational sensitivity (C67-C70) that are consistent with structural principles (buried residues tolerate hydrophobic substitutions, active sites are functionally constrained). The identification of active-site residues from mutational data alone (C71) demonstrates the utility of the approach. The generalizability is supported by similar patterns in other proteins (C72), though this is noted as unpublished. The method is logical and the patterns are well-documented in the figures.

results.result: Computational prediction of suppressor effects using Rosetta showed limited agreement with experimental results: only one of six experimentally identified pairs (L36A/M63L, -3.7 kcal/mol) was predicted to be stable. Rosetta showed a marked bias for aromatic substitutions not observed experimentally, likely due to overpacking. Excluding aromatic substitutions, Rosetta predictions were in reasonable qualitative agreement with experiment. FoldX predictions showed poorer agreement than Rosetta.
results.evaluation: The computational validation is thorough, comparing predictions from two different methods (Rosetta and FoldX) with experimental results (C181, C191). The poor quantitative agreement (C184-C185) is honestly reported, and a systematic bias is identified and explained (C187-C189). The conditional conclusion that Rosetta performs reasonably well after correcting for the aromatic bias (C190) is appropriately cautious. This demonstrates that suppressor data can be used to benchmark computational methods (C192), which is a valuable secondary finding.

results.result: The Rs parameter, which evaluates deviation from average accessible surface area, performed poorly for model discrimination: when the CcdB decoy set was sorted by Rs values, the native structure ranked 934th and the correlation between RMSD and Rs was only 0.3.
results.evaluation: The comparison with the Rs parameter provides context for evaluating ContactScore performance. The poor performance is clearly documented (C161) and demonstrates that simple accessibility-based metrics are insufficient for model discrimination in this system. This validates the need for the contact-based approach and strengthens the significance of the ContactScore results.

results.result: Proximal suppressors are expected to show complementary properties (e.g., large→small substitution compensated by small→large), with both individual mutations destabilizing in WT background but the pair showing increased stability (positive sign epistasis). Distal suppressors are expected to be on the protein surface with the individual suppressor mutation neutral in WT background and no complementarity in amino acid properties.
results.evaluation: These claims describe the theoretical framework underlying the suppressor classification approach. The expectations are based on sound structural and thermodynamic principles (C82-C84) and are supported by literature (C86). The framework is validated by the experimental results showing that proximal suppressors are indeed buried and in contact (C107), while distal suppressors are surface-exposed (C111). The theoretical predictions match the experimental observations.

results.result: SCA analysis found no interaction between R10 and L36, though this was limited by low sequence diversity of CcdB. Experimentally, R10G stabilized WT and multiple parent inactive mutants, while E11R stabilized V20F. The mechanism of R10G stabilization may involve the conformational flexibility of glycine allowing access to conformations not available to other residues, but further experiments are needed to understand E11R and confirm if it also functions as a global suppressor.
results.evaluation: The mechanistic understanding of global suppression is incomplete. The SCA analysis is negative (C139) but this is appropriately attributed to limited sequence diversity. The experimental observations are clear (C140-C141), but the proposed mechanism for R10G (C142) is speculative. The honest acknowledgment that further experiments are needed (C143) indicates this is preliminary mechanistic insight rather than a definitive explanation. The result identifies an interesting phenomenon but does not fully explain it.

results.result: The suppressor results for DgkA are consistent with a recent reanalysis of oriented sample solid state NMR data showing better agreement with the crystal than with the solution NMR structure.
results.evaluation: This claim provides independent validation of the DgkA conclusion from a different experimental technique (solid state NMR). The consistency between suppressor mutagenesis and solid state NMR strengthens confidence in the conclusion that the X-ray structure is the functional conformation. However, this is a supporting observation rather than a primary result of the study.
